A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same IEM research, with matching authors, core methods, and theoretical framework. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original perceptual-quality evaluations on TID2013, LIVE, CSIQ, TQD, and BAPPS, together with synthetic geometry and clustering experiments.

after.justification: V2 retains these empirical studies and adds PSNR-constrained image-optimization experiments on DIV2K, including aggregated results over 30 images.

M1.justification: The IEM definitions, denoiser architectures, and learned weighting function remain unchanged. Appendix D.3 adds an optimization adaptation: progressively optimizing the IEM integrand from low to high SNR using one noise sample per step and projecting distortions onto a fixed-PSNR constraint.

E1.justification: V2 adds DIV2K and a distinct evaluation scenario: actively minimizing or maximizing perceptual metrics while constraining distortion magnitude. This substantially extends evaluation beyond scoring existing image pairs to testing behavior under metric-driven image optimization; previous coverage is retained.

E2.justification: Comparator membership in the retained benchmark and clustering experiments is unchanged. The new optimization study reuses existing comparators: DISTS, LPIPS, VIF, SSIM, TOPIQ, PieAPP, NLPD, and GMSD. It introduces no new baseline algorithm.

E3.justification: The new study introduces projected optimization with 1,000 Adam steps at five PSNR constraints from 30 to 10 dB, plus aggregation over 30 images. Separately, Appendix E.4 changes the reported Laplace scales from (4, 2) to (0.3, 0.1) and widens its integration ranges. Existing MOS and BAPPS protocols are retained.

E4.justification: Section 3.3 and Appendix D.3 add substantial optimization stress tests examining structural preservation and artifacts under metric minimization and maximization. Figures 9–12 show outcomes across distortion levels, while Figure 13 checks whether each objective was effectively optimized. These supplement the retained disagreement examples and synthetic analyses.

E5.justification: Figure 13 newly reports means and standard-deviation error bars for initial, minimized, and maximized metric values across 30 randomly selected DIV2K images. This measures variation across images; it does not establish additional training seeds or repeated-run significance testing.

E6.justification: V2 adds qualitative optimization outcomes and quantitative initial/best/worst metric results. It also revises PieAPP scores throughout Figure 4 and the corresponding BAPPS, KRCC, and PLCC plots; for example, PieAPP moves above IEM on TID2013 SRCC. Existing IEM benchmark scores are unchanged. Figure 2's numerical geometry illustrations are also revised.

T1.justification: Equation (4) corrects the noise terms inside the squared norms from minus to plus. Theorem 2 now specifies expansion of the squared IEM, and the pointwise I-MMSE statement replaces 'any' realization with 'almost every' signal and Wiener trajectory. The principal theorems and proof framework remain intact.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the same central metric, geometric, and perceptual-prediction claims. Section 3.3 adds the more specific claim that IEM may serve as a robust standalone optimization objective, extending v1's general discussion of optimization as a potential future application.

C2.justification: V2 interprets the new optimization results as supporting structural preservation and sensitivity to perturbations outside the data support. Appendix D.3 explains low-SNR gradient scale and variance as optimization difficulties, and Figure 13 qualifies that global optima are not guaranteed. Existing computational-cost and hyperparameter-selection limitations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix D.3 supplies optimization hyperparameters, SNR endpoints, projection instructions, DIV2K preprocessing, and the IQA-PyTorch implementation source. Appendix E.4 revises illustrative computation parameters. The existing architecture/training tables and code-access information are retained.

R1.justification: V2 replaces the Ma et al. (2018) group-maximum-differentiation citation with Wang and Simoncelli (2008), and adds references for DIV2K and IQA-PyTorch. The broader positioning against metric learning, information geometry, and score-derived Riemannian metrics remains unchanged.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the overall narrative structure are preserved. V2 adds dedicated maximum-differentiation subsections, makes localized wording and proof-explanation edits, updates cross-references, and adds the conference-publication header.

P2.justification: V2 adds the explanatory Figure 5, four optimization image grids in Figures 9–12, and the multi-panel error-bar Figure 13. Figure 2 is redrawn and several benchmark axes are rescaled. Earlier appendix figures and both tables are retained with renumbering or relocation.

improvement.justification: V2 improves empirical scrutiny through documented optimization stress tests and 30-image variability reporting, while correcting mathematical errors such as Equation (4). The gains are limited: the new perceptual-quality conclusions lack additional human validation, and substantial PieAPP score revisions are unexplained. These tradeoffs support a modest net improvement rather than a fundamental strengthening of the paper.
